summary.text: Case 2 is a liver transplant recipient (transplanted for PSC) in whom de novo UC-type IBD developed 65.7 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, bloody stool, abdominal pain and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was Mayo 9.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis recorded the extent of disease as pancolitis in Table 3, with endoscopic severity MES 3/UCEIS 6 and moderate histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Case 2 initially received 5-ASA 4 g with insufficient response, and corticosteroids (prednisolone 30 mg) were subsequently required, resulting in clinical and endoscopic remission. Remission was maintained on the baseline immunosuppressive regimen without additional IBD-specific therapy.
Follow-up lasted 12.0 months with no adverse events, stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Routine post-transplant cancer surveillance was recommended for all transplant recipients.

summary.text: Case 3 is a liver transplant recipient (transplanted for PSC) in whom de novo UC-type IBD developed 64.1 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, bloody stool, abdominal pain and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was Mayo 11.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis recorded the extent of disease as pancolitis in Table 3, with endoscopic severity MES 3/UCEIS 8 and severe histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Case 3 presented with severe, rapidly progressive pancolitis with multiple deep ulcers. Corticosteroids were initiated but proved ineffective, and early escalation to mirikizumab was required, leading to clinical and endoscopic remission; the biologic was continued as maintenance after induction.
Follow-up lasted 5.1 months with no adverse events, stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Routine post-transplant cancer surveillance was recommended for all transplant recipients.

summary.text: Case 4 is a heart transplant recipient (transplanted for DCM) in whom de novo CD-like IBD developed 30.8 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was CDAI 327.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis showed extent recorded as pancolitis in Table 3 and segmental inflammation with skip lesions in the narrative, a source conflict kept for review, with endoscopic severity SES-CD 19 and severe histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Systemic corticosteroids were avoided after discussion with the transplant team, and ustekinumab was used as first-line biologic induction, with first-line outcome recorded as remission and clinical improvement described. Thiopurines could not be added because of concomitant MMF therapy.
Follow-up lasted 38.2 months with no adverse events, stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Routine post-transplant cancer surveillance was recommended for all transplant recipients.

summary.text: Case 5 is a heart transplant recipient (transplanted for DCM) in whom de novo CD-like IBD developed 9.7 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, bloody stool, abdominal pain and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was CDAI 201.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis recorded the extent of disease as cecum in Table 3, with endoscopic severity SES-CD 8 and moderate histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Systemic corticosteroids were avoided after discussion with the transplant team, and risankizumab was used as first-line biologic induction, with first-line outcome recorded as remission and clinical improvement described. Thiopurines could not be added because of concomitant MMF therapy.
Follow-up lasted 18.7 months with no adverse events, stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Routine post-transplant cancer surveillance was recommended for all transplant recipients.

summary.text: Case 6 is a heart transplant recipient (transplanted for IHD) in whom de novo CD-like IBD developed 162.2 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, abdominal pain and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was CDAI 295.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis showed extent recorded as pancolitis in Table 3 and segmental inflammation with skip lesions in the narrative, a source conflict kept for review, with endoscopic severity SES-CD 37 and moderate histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Systemic corticosteroids were avoided after discussion with the transplant team, and risankizumab was used as first-line biologic induction, with first-line outcome recorded as partial response and clinical improvement described. Thiopurines could not be added because of concomitant MMF therapy.
Follow-up lasted 12.5 months with stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Acute myeloid leukemia developed during follow-up, although its relationship to biologic therapy remains unclear.

summary.text: Case 1 is a liver transplant recipient (transplanted for PSC) in whom de novo UC-type IBD developed 262.2 months after transplantation. At onset the patient presented with diarrhea, bloody stool, abdominal pain and was receiving a tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive regimen. No intestinal symptoms had been present before transplantation. The clinical severity score was Mayo 8.

Colonoscopy at IBD diagnosis recorded the extent of disease as pancolitis in Table 3, with endoscopic severity MES 3/UCEIS 7 and severe histological severity. CMV immunohistochemistry was negative, and CMV colitis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder were reported as excluded, while drug-induced colitis was described both as excluded and as not definitively excluded.

Case 1 initially received 5-ASA 4 g with insufficient response, and corticosteroids (prednisolone 25 mg) were subsequently required, resulting in clinical and endoscopic remission. Remission was maintained on the baseline immunosuppressive regimen without additional IBD-specific therapy.
Follow-up lasted 21.9 months with no adverse events, stable graft function and no IBD-related surgery. Routine post-transplant cancer surveillance was recommended for all transplant recipients.
